## Q11

**Answer:**
**What the final rule says about cost.** The rule sets **no dollar amount**. It directs applicants to pay "the required fees" and "the appropriate fee" as prescribed by USCIS in the form instructions — 8 CFR 214.1(c)(2) ("together with the required fees and all initial evidence specified in the applicable provisions of Sec. 214.2, and in the form instructions, including the submission of any biometrics required by 8 CFR 103.16") and 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(A) ("remitting the appropriate fee"), with parallel language for F-2 dependents at 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iv). DHS explains that it replaced specific form names with general language precisely so that form changes would not require rulemaking, and that USCIS conducts biennial fee studies and "will allocate appropriate levels of resources to ensure the adjudication of EOS continues in a timely fashion" (91 FR 45083). The dollar figures that appear in the Federal Register document are **not** agency-set fee amounts: commenters cited a **$420** Form I-539 fee (91 FR 45055) and "**$555 per application including biometrics**" (91 FR 45065); DHS used a **$490** average figure for legal help with an I-539 from the form's supporting statement (91 FR 45083); and the Regulatory Impact Analysis computed an average total cost of an EOS request of **$732 to $1,311** "depending on the level of assistance and submission method" (91 FR 45090, in the I-nonimmigrant discussion).

**What the final rule says about how long USCIS takes.** Again, no deadline or service-level commitment. DHS states: "**DHS cannot guarantee processing times** for applications filed at USCIS due to numerous governing factors" (91 FR 45025), and it declined commenters' requests to publish service-level targets, set a 90-day adjudication timeline, or grant automatic interim approvals (91 FR 45021, 45024). The only timing the rule guarantees is the applicant's own protection while waiting: **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii)** gives authorized stay until USCIS decides, and auto-extends current on-campus, CPT and severe economic hardship employment for **up to 240 days** from the I-94 admit-until date. Commenters cited observed processing times (3.5 months for extensions and 4.5 months for F-1/J-1 changes of status at one service center, 91 FR 45083; more than 6.5 months to adjudicate 80% of EOS requests, 91 FR 45063), but those are commenter statements, not agency findings.

**Handout language (accurate, two sentences):** "An extension of stay is filed on Form I-539. The rule itself sets no fee and no processing deadline: the fee is whatever the current USCIS form instructions require (and biometrics may be required), and USCIS has said it cannot guarantee how long a decision will take — but if you file before your I-94 expires you may stay while the application is pending, and on-campus or CPT work continues automatically for up to 240 days."

**Basis:**
8 CFR 214.1(c)(2), 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(A), (f)(7)(iv), (f)(5)(viii) as added/amended by 2026-14439 (91 FR 45122, 45126, 45125–45126); 91 FR 45021, 45024, 45025, 45055, 45065, 45083, 45090; PRA discussion at 91 FR 45120 (no fee stated; 1.667-hour burden for paper I-539, 1 hour for e-file, 1.17 hours for biometrics).

**Uncertainty:**
Because the rule deliberately defers to the form instructions and the USCIS fee schedule, an adviser must check the current I-539 instructions for the actual fee; any dollar figure attributed to "the rule" would be wrong. Likewise, no processing-time figure in the document is an agency commitment.

## Q12

**Answer:**
**(a) Is an I-539 received during the 60 days after the I-20 program end date timely? Yes — most defensibly, yes.** 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B) makes an extension application timely "if the receipt date, pursuant to 8 CFR 103.2(a)(7), is on or before the date the authorized period of stay expires, **which includes the 30-day period provided in paragraph (f)(5)(v)**," and repeats that "USCIS must receive the extension application on or before the expiration of the authorized period of stay, including the 30-day period … allowed after the completion of studies or any authorized practical training." For a D/S-transition student like Priya, 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1) makes the **60-day** departure period part of the authorized period of stay itself ("authorized to remain … until the later date of … the program end date noted on their Form I-20 … plus the departure period of 60 days for F nonimmigrants"), and 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(i) itself refers to filings made "including the 60 day departure period." So an I-539 received on or before **July 14, 2027** (May 15, 2027 + 60 days) should be timely. That said, the operative timely-filing sentence in (f)(7)(iii)(B) speaks of "the 30-day period provided in paragraph (f)(5)(v)," and the transition paragraph supplies 60 days; the mismatch is textual, not resolved expressly.

**(b) If she files during those 60 days, does she keep the automatic extension of on-campus or CPT employment? No.** 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii) extends current on-campus, CPT and severe economic hardship employment "during the pendency of the extension of stay application," but expressly provides: "**If an F-1 student files an extension of stay application during the 30-day period provided in paragraph (f)(5)(v) of this section, he or she does not receive an automatic extension of authorized employment**, including on-campus, CPT, and severe economic hardship, and must wait for approval of the extension of stay application (and employment authorization application, if required) before engaging in CPT or employment." The preamble says the same flatly: "all employment must cease if the EOS application is filed after the F-1 completes their course of study and any authorized post-completion practical training, **including during the departure period**" (91 FR 45027). She does keep authorized stay (up to USCIS's decision, 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii)) and may continue a full course of study if she is still enrolled (8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B)).

**(c) Recommendation for the adviser.** Advise Priya to file the I-539 **on or before her I-20 program end date (May 15, 2027)** — not during the 60 days — if she has (or wants to preserve) any on-campus or CPT work; filing early is not prohibited and there is no earliest-filing rule (91 FR 45040 n.197: "there is no prohibition on filing the form before a certain date ahead of expiration"). Filing in the 60-day window remains timely and preserves lawful stay, but she must stop all work until approval, so it should be presented as a fallback rather than a plan. If her goal is OPT rather than an extension of study, point her to the different route in 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(i): an I-765 filed **on or before March 18, 2027** and before her admission expires exempts her from the I-539 altogether and, if approved, gives stay through the EAD end date plus 60 days.

**Basis:**
8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B), (f)(5)(viii), (f)(5)(v) (91 FR 45125–45126); 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1), (m)(1)(i) (91 FR 45122–45123); preamble at 91 FR 45027 (employment must cease), 91 FR 45040 n.197 (no earliest filing date); June 2027 arithmetic: May 15, 2027 + 60 days = July 14, 2027.

**Uncertainty:**
Whether USCIS will read the "30-day period" cross-reference in (f)(7)(iii)(B) to include the transition cohort's 60-day period is not stated in the rule. The risk is asymmetric: if USCIS read the window as 30 days, and receipt fell between day 31 and day 60, only the employment auto-extension question is clearly resolved by the text; the timeliness question would be contested. That is a further reason to file before the program end date.

## Q13

**Answer:**
**(a) After her January 9, 2027 return: through June 13, 2027.** Her D/S admission on September 15, 2026 was converted into a **new fixed admission** when she traveled: the preamble states that "the admission period of any F or J nonimmigrant previously admitted for D/S will be transitioned to a fixed date of admission **upon travel outside the United States**" and that such travelers "may be admitted with a new fixed admission period … as provided for in new 8 CFR 214.1(a)(4), based on the date on their Form I-20 … and 30 days for departure" (91 FR 45099, 45100). Under **8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A)** CBP admits for the shorter of 4 years or the program length on the I-20, plus 30 days; **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)** caps the admission at the program length and adds "an additional 30 days as provided in paragraph (f)(5)(v)," which in turn provides that the 30-day period "will be reflected on the F-1 student's … Form I-94." Arithmetic: program end **May 14, 2027** + 30 days = May 31 (17 days) + **June 13, 2027** (30 days). Note the contrast: had she **not** traveled, 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1) would have protected her to May 14, 2027 + **60** days = July 13, 2027. Her trip cost her the extra 30 days.

**(b) Is a Form I-539 needed for the OPT period, and by when?** **Yes.** She falls in the specific carve-out in **8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(ii)**: "An F-1 student described in this paragraph (m)(1) who **departs the United States before filing the application for post-completion OPT** … and **is admitted to the United States with a fixed period of admission** is required to file **both** an Application for Employment Authorization, Form I-765, … **and** an Application to Extend/Change Nonimmigrant Status, Form I-539." She left on December 19, 2026, filed the I-765 on February 22, 2027, and was readmitted on January 9, 2027 with a fixed admission — squarely within that paragraph. **Deadline:** USCIS must receive the I-539 on or before the expiration of her authorized period of stay, **June 13, 2027** (8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B)). (If she prefers, 8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(D) allows her instead to "seek admission through CBP after travel abroad" rather than filing an EOS — see (d) below — but she cannot simply stay without one or the other.)

**(c) If everything is approved as requested, how long may she stay?** **Through July 9, 2028.** The OPT EAD requested runs June 10, 2027–June 9, 2028. Because she must obtain an extension of stay (she is outside the 214.1(m)(1)(i) exemption), **8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(D)** provides that "if the application for post-completion OPT is granted along with an extension of stay … the student extension will include **the additional 30-day period** provided in paragraph (f)(5)(v) for departure following the expiration of the time approved to complete post-completion OPT" (consistent with the 4-year-maximum extension rule in 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(vi)). June 9, 2028 + 30 days = June 30 (21 days) + **July 9, 2028** (30 days).

**(d) Alternative facts (no December travel; I-765 pending; trip May 20–June 5, 2027).** **No Form I-539 is required.** She filed the I-765 on February 22, 2027 — before her period of admission expired and **on or before March 18, 2027** — so **8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(i)** exempts her from filing an I-539 "for the requested period of post-completion OPT"; the (m)(1)(ii) both-filings requirement applies only to students who depart **before** filing the OPT application, which she did not. **Period of admission on return:** **8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(iii)** provides that an F-1 seeking admission to pursue post-completion OPT "may be admitted until the end date of the approved employment authorization … or, if the Application for Employment Authorization … is still pending with USCIS, as evidenced by a notice issued by USCIS indicating receipt of such application, **until the Designated School Official's recommended employment end date for post-completion OPT … specified on the Form I-20**, subject to the requirements in paragraph (c)(8) … plus a 30-day period." With the I-765 pending on June 5, 2027, she may be admitted to the DSO's recommended OPT end date (June 9, 2028) **plus 30 days = July 9, 2028**. **What she should carry:** her **Form I-797C receipt notice** for the I-765, and her **I-20 endorsed by the DSO recommending OPT with the proposed dates** — 8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(iii); 8 CFR 214.1(c)(8)(iii) ("should travel with a copy of their Form I-797C … along with proposed length of stay as evidenced by the Form I-20"); preamble at 91 FR 45099 (aliens "should have a notice … issued by USCIS indicating receipt of the application for employment authorization … and their latest I-20 endorsed by their DSO approving OPT … with a proposed end date").

**Basis:**
8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A), (a)(4)(iii) (91 FR 45122); 8 CFR 214.1(c)(8)(iii) (91 FR 45123); 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(i), (m)(1)(ii) (91 FR 45122–45123); 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i), (f)(5)(v), (f)(7)(iii)(B), (f)(7)(vi), (f)(10)(ii)(D) (91 FR 45124–45126); preamble at 91 FR 45098–45100.

**Uncertainty:**
For (a): whether a re-admission on the same I-20 with no change of program end date nonetheless "drops" the transition cohort's 60-day period to 30 days is my reading of the preamble's statement that the transition to a fixed date happens "upon travel outside the United States"; the rule does not say in terms that the traveler loses the extra 30 days, and a CBP officer who admitted her consistently with 214.1(m)(1) could instead have issued an I-94 running to July 13, 2027. For (d): the admission "until the DSO's recommended employment end date … plus 30 days" presumes the I-765 is still pending at the port of entry; if it had been approved, the admit-until date would be the EAD end date plus 30 days.

## Q14

**Answer:**
**(a) The document behind the report.** **FR Doc. 2026-20660, "Optional Practical Training Fees," notice of proposed rulemaking, 91 FR 64566–64600, published October 8, 2026.** Agency: **Department of Homeland Security, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)**. Docket: **DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100**. RIN: **1653-AB01**. Affects 8 CFR part 214 (proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(i)–(iii) and new 8 CFR 214.13(i)). **Status: proposed only; not in force.** Deadlines it sets: comments on the rule **on or before November 9, 2026** (closed); comments on the information collection **by December 7, 2026**; and, as proposed, the fee would apply to DSO recommendations dated **on or after the date 60 days after publication of any final rule** (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(3)). No final rule or correction appears through November 14, 2026.

**(b) If finalized and in effect before the DSO's April 2027 recommendation, which amount applies to Daniel's STEM OPT extension?** **$30,000 — the "subsequent OPT" fee — is the most defensible reading, but the proposed text leaves a gap for his situation.** The amounts are set out in proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)–(2): a school must pay "a one-time initial fee of **$70,000** for each F-1 student the first time that the alien is recommended to participate in OPT," and "**$30,000** for each F-1 student prior to a **subsequent** recommendation of the alien to participate in OPT … if the alien has previously participated in OPT and paid the initial OPT fee of $70,000." DHS's explanation is explicit that the $30,000 covers "any type of OPT that an F-1 student participates in after having completed their initial OPT (regardless of whether it is another pre-completion OPT, post-completion OPT, **or STEM OPT extension**)" (91 FR 64577). Daniel has already participated in (indeed, is on) his initial post-completion OPT, so his STEM OPT recommendation is a "subsequent" OPT recommendation → $30,000. The gap: the literal condition requires that he "ha[s] previously … paid the initial OPT fee of $70,000," which his school never did because his initial OPT predates the rule; the transition paragraph has the same condition ("for which the $70,000 OPT fee has been paid"), and the NPRM nowhere addresses a student whose first OPT predates the fee. The $70,000 would not apply, because it is expressly a one-time "first time" fee.

**(c) Who pays, when, what follows a failure to pay, and is it refundable?** **The school pays — not the student.** "An **SEVP-certified educational institution** must pay" (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)–(2)); the payment "must be made **prior to the DSO recommending a student for OPT**" and "prior to the DSO entering the OPT recommendation in SEVIS" (91 FR 64577). The DSO must confirm payment, update SEVIS with the fee payment information, and give the student a signed, dated I-20 showing the recommendation and confirming payment (proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(i), (ii)(B)–(C)). **If not paid:** the DSO "may not enter the OPT recommendation in SEVIS if the OPT fee has not yet been paid," and "USCIS would not grant employment authorization to any student where the school has failed to pay the applicable OPT fee prior to issuing an OPT recommendation or … completely failed to pay" (proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(iii); 91 FR 64577). **Refunds:** only on a case-by-case discretionary SEVP determination, and only if the student "has not been issued the employment authorization document" for the OPT (or OPT extension) associated with the fee; the DSO must first remove the OPT recommendation in SEVIS; "this fee will not be refunded under any circumstances once the F-1 student has been granted the employment authorization document"; refund determinations "are not subject to any administrative appeals" (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)–(2)).

**(d) From when would the fee apply; could timing keep Daniel outside it?** Proposed **8 CFR 214.13(i)(3)** ("Transition period"): schools "must pay the fee of $70,000 for each alien who receives a DSO recommendation for OPT that is **dated on or after [60 days after date of publication of the final rule]**," and thereafter "any subsequent DSO recommendations for OPT issued for any F-1 student who has previously participated in OPT … will be subject to the subsequent OPT fee of $30,000." So the trigger is **the date of the DSO's recommendation**, not the date of the I-765 or of employment. **Yes — timing could keep him outside it:** if his DSO issues the STEM OPT recommendation in April 2027 and the final rule is not yet effective on that date, no fee applies to that recommendation. Since a final rule must be published and then 60 days must run, a recommendation dated April 2027 would escape the fee unless a final rule had been published by roughly mid-February 2027 — and no final rule has been published as of November 14, 2026. This is a timing bet, not a guarantee: DHS could publish a final rule at any time.

**(e) Under the rules in force today, what must Daniel file for the STEM OPT period, what happens to his work authorization, and until when may he stay?** He must file **both** a **Form I-765** (STEM OPT extension) **and a Form I-539 extension of stay**. He is outside the March 18, 2027 exemption: 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(i) exempts from the I-539 only an F-1 recommended for STEM OPT who files the I-765 "prior to the expiration of his or her current OPT EAD … **on or before March 18, 2027**"; Daniel files **April 12, 2027**, so the exemption is unavailable. That is confirmed by the general rule in **8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(D)**: "**Unless described in Sec. 214.1(m)(1)(i)**, an F-1 student recommended for post-completion OPT must apply for an employment authorization **and either apply for an extension of stay with USCIS or seek admission through CBP after travel abroad**, and may not engage in post-completion OPT unless such employment authorization is granted." **Work authorization while pending:** 8 CFR 274a.12(b)(6)(iv) gives a **180-day automatic extension** of his post-completion OPT EAD while the STEM OPT I-765 is pending if it was timely filed — confirmed at 91 FR 45037 and 45101 ("eligible F-1 nonimmigrants who have timely applied for the 24-month STEM OPT extension will benefit from the automatic extension of employment until the date of USCIS' written decision on the Form I-765, but not to exceed 180 days"). 180 days from June 30, 2027 = July 31 (31) + Aug 31 (62) + Sep 30 (92) + Oct 31 (123) + Nov 30 (153) + **December 27, 2027** (180). His authorized stay while the I-539 is pending is protected by 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii) (until decision). **If approved:** the STEM OPT EAD would run 24 months past June 30, 2027, i.e., to **June 30, 2029**, and because the extension of stay is granted with the OPT, 8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(D) adds the 30-day departure period → **July 30, 2029** (consistent with 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(vi), which caps an extension at 4 years and excludes the 30-day periods from the maximum).

**Basis:**
2026-20660 (91 FR 64566; DATES at 91 FR 64566; discussion at 91 FR 64576–64577; proposed regulatory text at 91 FR 64599–64600, i.e., proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11) and 214.13(i)(1)–(3)); 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(i) (91 FR 45123); 8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(D) (91 FR 45126); 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii), (f)(7)(vi) (91 FR 45125–45126); 8 CFR 274a.12(b)(6)(iv); 91 FR 45037, 45046, 45101 (180-day STEM OPT auto-extension).

**Uncertainty:**
On (b): the proposed text conditions the $30,000 on prior payment of the $70,000, which will not be true for students already on OPT when the rule takes effect, and DHS did not address this transition case — a final rule could either clarify that the $30,000 applies or extend the $70,000 to a first recommendation after the effective date. On (e): the 180-day auto-extension depends on the I-765 being timely filed relative to the OPT EAD expiration (June 30, 2027); the current 90-day STEM OPT filing window is not restated in 2026-14439 and should be checked in the then-current form instructions.

## Q15

**Answer:**
**1. "USCIS must receive an extension-of-stay application before the program end date on the student's I-20." — INCORRECT as a statement of timely filing (correct only as advice for preserving work).** 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B) makes an application timely if USCIS receives it "on or before the date the authorized period of stay expires, **which includes the 30-day period provided in paragraph (f)(5)(v)**" — so receipt up to the I-94 admit-until date (program end + 30 days) is timely. What is lost by filing after the program end date is **employment**: 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii) (filing "during the 30-day period … does not receive an automatic extension of authorized employment"), reinforced by 91 FR 45027. **Reworded:** "To keep working without a break, USCIS must receive your Form I-539 by the program end date on your I-20; a filing after that date but by the end of your 30-day departure period is still timely, but all work must stop until it is approved."

**2. "The four-year maximum period of admission is counted from the day the student enters the United States." — INCORRECT.** The regulatory text (8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A); 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)) sets a 4-year maximum and excludes the 30-day arrival and departure windows, but does not state the start point. The preamble resolves it: "the calculation of the 4-year maximum period of admission **will not begin from the date of admission during that 30-day arrival window, but from the program start date**," and the 30-day departure periods "will not count towards the 4-year maximum" (91 FR 45098; repeated at 91 FR 45016). **Reworded:** "The four-year maximum runs from the program start date on the I-20, and the 30 days allowed before the program start and after the program end do not count against it." *(Text/preamble note: here the text is silent rather than contrary; the preamble supplies the method and should control practice, though the text is what is enforceable.)*

**3. "If USCIS has still not decided a timely filed extension application 240 days after the I-94 date, the student may stay and keep studying but must stop any on-campus job." — CORRECT (with one condition).** 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii) provides that a student whose I-94 has expired "will be considered to be in a period of authorized stay" if he or she timely filed an extension "until USCIS issues a decision," and separately caps the automatic extension of on-campus/CPT/severe-hardship employment at "240 days beginning from the end date of his or her period of admission as indicated on the … Form I-94." The Summary of Changes confirms the stay-and-study half: DHS is "codifying that an F-1 student who has timely filed an EOS application, will be authorized to continue pursuing a full course of study after the expiration of the admission period until USCIS adjudicates the EOS application" (91 FR 44978). Condition: the employment auto-extension is available only if the application was filed **before** the departure period began — filing during the departure period forfeits it entirely (same paragraph). No further filing is required for F-1 students (unlike J-1 and I, which must file a subsequent request). **Minor reword:** "…may stay and keep studying, but on-campus/CPT work stops after the 240-day mark (and never starts if the application was filed after the program end date)."

**4. "A student in an English language training program who falls seriously ill can extend beyond 24 months on medical grounds." — INCORRECT.** 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)(A) restricts ELT students to "a maximum of admission period of **24 months**, plus an additional 30-day period of stay," and DHS addressed the medical point directly: "Students who encounter extenuating circumstances such as **illness, disability, or other emergencies** during their studies, **will still be limited to the 24-month admission period**" (91 FR 45039; see also 91 FR 45038, 45013). The general medical-extension ground in 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(i)(C)(2)(ii) does not override the ELT cap. **Reworded:** "English-language students are capped at 24 months of language study in the aggregate, and illness or another emergency does not extend that cap; F-1 students admitted for other programs may, however, continue English study during their stay."

**5. "A degree program accredited as a five-year program has to be shortened, or issued on two I-20s, to fit the four-year limit." — INCORRECT.** DHS rejected exactly this: "The commenters are mistaken when they think that accredited programs will need to be shortened to fit the 4-year admission period. **That is untrue.** If the program has been accredited as a 5-year program, the I-20 … will state the full program length. The student will need to apply for an EOS with USCIS prior to the expiration of his or her currently authorized period of stay using the same I-20 … and **may continue to study while the application is pending**" (91 FR 45039–45040). **Reworded:** "A five-year accredited program stays on one I-20 showing the full length; the student applies for an extension of stay before the four-year admission expires and may keep studying while it is pending." *(Text/preamble note: the 4-year cap in 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i) is a cap on the admission, not on the program; the preamble states how DHS will apply it, and there is no contrary text.)*

**6. "A student who travels abroad and is readmitted on an I-20 with a later program end date gets a new admission period from CBP, and then does not need an extension of stay from USCIS for that time." — PARTLY CORRECT.** The first half is right: 8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A) lets CBP admit for the shorter of 4 years or the program length plus 30 days, and the preamble confirms that D/S admission "will be transitioned to a fixed date of admission upon travel outside the United States" and that such travelers "may be admitted with a new fixed admission period" (91 FR 45099–45100). The second half is only true if the new admission actually covers the remaining program: because the 4-year maximum is counted **from the program start date** (91 FR 45098), a re-admission late in a long program may produce an admit-until date that does not reach the program end, in which case an EOS is still required (8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(iv); 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)). Two caveats: if an EOS was pending, seeking admission on the I-20 with the later end date may cause it to be **deemed abandoned** and the new I-94 to govern (8 CFR 214.1(c)(8)(ii); 91 FR 45098–45099); and a departure/absence of more than five months requires initial-status admission (91 FR 45048). **Reworded:** "Travel and re-entry gives you a new fixed admission period, but it is capped at four years from your program start date plus 30 days — if your program runs longer, you still need an extension of stay." *(Text/preamble note: 8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A) does not state when the four years begins; the preamble's calculation method (91 FR 45098) supplies it and, being the agency's stated interpretation of its own rule, governs practice, but the text is the enforceable rule and CBP retains discretion.)*

**7. "The exemption from filing Form I-539 for OPT applicants covers I-765s filed within six months of the rule's effective date, so the last filing day is March 15, 2027." — INCORRECT.** The final rule uses a fixed date, not a six-month computation: 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(i) exempts a post-completion OPT applicant who files the I-765 "before his or her period of admission expires, including the 60 day departure period … **on or before March 18, 2027**," and a STEM OPT applicant who files "prior to the expiration of his or her current OPT Employment Authorization Document … **on or before March 18, 2027**." The same March 18, 2027 date governs the J-1 parallel provisions (8 CFR 214.2(j)(1)(vii)). March 15, 2027 (six months after the September 15, 2026 effective date) is not the operative date. DHS may extend the exemption "beyond March 18, 2027, in 6-month increments by publication of a notification in the Federal Register" (8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(iii)). **Reworded:** "If you are recommended for post-completion OPT and file your Form I-765 on or before March 18, 2027 (and before your authorized stay expires), you do not need a separate Form I-539 for that OPT period; for STEM OPT the same March 18, 2027 deadline applies and the I-765 must also be filed before your current OPT EAD expires."

**Basis:**
8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B), (f)(5)(viii), (f)(5)(v), (f)(5)(i)(A), (f)(5)(i), (f)(8)(iv), (f)(7)(i)(C)(2)(ii) (91 FR 45124–45127); 8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A), 214.1(c)(8)(ii), 214.1(m)(1)(i), (m)(1)(iii) (91 FR 45122–45123); 8 CFR 214.2(j)(1)(vii) (91 FR 45130); preamble at 91 FR 44978, 45013, 45016, 45027, 45038–45040, 45048, 45098–45099.

**Uncertainty:**
Items 2 and 6 are the places where the regulatory text is silent (no start point for the 4-year clock) and the preamble supplies the rule; an adjudicator or CBP officer applying the text alone could compute the four years differently, and the preamble's method is not binding in the way the text is. Item 3's answer assumes the EOS was filed before the departure period began; filed later, the employment protection is zero rather than 240 days.

## Q16

**Answer:**
**(a) Lin's admit-until date: September 22, 2031.** 8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A) admits an F-1 for "a maximum period of 4 years or the length of program as specified on Form I-20, whichever is shorter, plus additional 30 day periods for arrival and departure as provided in Sec. 214.2(f)(5)(i)." Her program (Aug 23, 2027–May 14, 2033) is about 5 years 9 months, so the 4-year maximum controls, and 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i) tells us what does not count: "The 30-day period before the indicated report date or program start date and 30 additional days following the program end date or the 4-year maximum period of admission do not count toward the maximum length of stay." The preamble fixes the start point: "the calculation of the 4-year maximum period of admission will not begin from the date of admission during that 30-day arrival window, but from the program start date" (91 FR 45098; see also 91 FR 45016). Arithmetic: program start **Aug 23, 2027** + 4 years = **Aug 23, 2031**; + 30-day departure period = Aug 31 (8 days) + **Sept 22, 2031** (30 days). Her Aug 2, 2027 entry date does not move the date (if it did, the result would be Sept 1, 2031).

**(b) What she must do to stay beyond that date.** She must file a **Form I-539 application for extension of stay** with USCIS before her authorized period of stay expires. **What she submits** (8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(ii)–(iii)(A)): the updated, **properly endorsed Form I-20 bearing the DSO's recommendation and new program end date**; **evidence of sufficient funds** to cover expenses; appearance for any **biometrics** required by 8 CFR 103.16; and **the appropriate fee**; she must be maintaining status and never have engaged in unauthorized employment (8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(A)). F-2 dependents must be included on her application or file their own (8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iv)). **Grounds on which it can be granted** (8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(i)): she has continually maintained lawful status (A), is pursuing a full course of study (B), and has either **(C)(1) a currently issued Form I-20 indicating additional time is left to complete the program** — which is her situation, since the I-20 shows May 14, 2033 — or (C)(2) documentation of a compelling academic reason, a compelling medical reason, or circumstances beyond her control. **How early may she file:** there is **no earliest filing date** — DHS states in a footnote to this very discussion: "With respect to the earliest filing date for a Form I-539, there is **no prohibition on filing the form before a certain date ahead of expiration**" (91 FR 45040 n.197). The outer limit is the **last day of her authorized stay, September 22, 2031** (8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B)). **If granted in full:** 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(vi) grants the extension "for the period of time necessary to complete the program as listed on the F-1 student's Form I-20 … **not to exceed 4 years**," with the 30-day periods not counting against the maximum; program end **May 14, 2033** + 30 days = May 31 (17 days) + **June 13, 2033** (30 days).

**(c) The 2029 master's en route to the PhD.** It does **not** affect her ability to finish the PhD. The same-or-lower-level bar in 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(C) is level-relative: it prohibits F-1 status "through a program at the **same** educational level or a **lower** educational level" than a program already completed. A PhD is a **higher** educational level than the master's, and 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(B) expressly provides that a student "who has completed a program … at one educational level and begins a new program at a **higher** educational level is considered to be maintaining F-1 status." Nor is the en-route master's a "change in educational objectives" requiring a new filing: she remains in the same PhD program of study listed on her I-20, and 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(A)'s graduate-level bar targets changes of objective and transfers **during** the program, not the award of a degree within it. The only practical consequence is that the master's completion date may be relevant if she later wants a new program at the same or a lower level (which would then be barred) or OPT at that level.

**(d) August 2030 re-entry on her I-20, no EOS pending.** 8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A) governs: CBP may admit her for the shorter of 4 years or the program length on the I-20, plus 30 days. **Most defensible answer: she is admitted only to September 22, 2031 — the same date she already had — so a mid-program re-entry does not cure the need for the Form I-539 in (b), and she must still file it.** This follows from the preamble's method of counting the four years from the program start date (Aug 23, 2027) rather than from any later admission (91 FR 45098), and from the rule's overall design, under which a program longer than four years requires an extension (8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i), (f)(7); 8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(iv)). **Certainty: low to moderate.** The text of 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A) does not say when the four years begins, and CBP has discretion (the operative verb is "may be admitted"); an officer who computes four years from the new date of admission (Aug 2030 → Aug 2034) and compares it with the program end (May 14, 2033) would instead admit her to **June 13, 2033**, which would make the EOS unnecessary for the remainder of the program. An adviser should assume the EOS is required and confirm the I-94 date at each re-entry.

**(e) The husband's separate 2031 travel, later I-94 date, and the fee.** **Until when may he stay:** the later I-94 date does not enlarge his stay. 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)(E) provides that "the authorized period of stay for F-2 dependents **may not exceed the authorized period of stay of the principal F-1 student**" (and 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(vi) repeats that extensions of stay for F-2 dependents may not exceed the F-1's authorized admission period). So he may stay only until Lin's authorized stay ends — **September 22, 2031** as admitted, or **June 13, 2033** if her extension is granted through the program end. He should not rely on the later I-94 date. **How he is covered when Lin applies:** 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iv) — "An F-2 spouse … seeking to accompany the principal F-1 student during the additional period of admission must **either be included on the principal F-1 student's application** for an extension of stay **or file their own** extension of stay application on the form designated by USCIS," with the same endorsed I-20, funds evidence, biometrics and fee, and proof of the qualifying relationship. **The fee:** the rule requires "remitting the appropriate fee" in either case (8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iv)), and DHS explains the mechanics: "If the dependent files a separate Form I-539, he or she will need to pay a **separate** Form I-539 filing fee. However, if the dependent files a **Form I-539A** as part of the primary applicant's EOS request on a Form I-539, **only one fee** will be required" (91 FR 45110; see also 91 FR 45013: "The Form I-539 allows dependents … to be included for one fee and concurrent adjudication"). Also note 8 CFR 214.1(c)(2): co-applicants in a single family unit holding derivative status may be included in one application, and "extensions granted to members of a family unit must be for the same period of time. The shortest period granted to any member of the family will be granted to all members."

**Basis:**
8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A) (91 FR 45122); 8 CFR 214.1(c)(2) (91 FR 45122–45123); 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i), (f)(5)(i)(E), (f)(5)(ii)(A)–(C), (f)(7)(i), (f)(7)(ii), (f)(7)(iii)(A)–(B), (f)(7)(iv), (f)(7)(vi), (f)(8)(iv) (91 FR 45124–45127); preamble at 91 FR 45013, 45016, 45040 n.197, 45098, 45110.

**Uncertainty:**
The 4-year start date is stated only in the preamble, not in the regulatory text, and no provision addresses a re-admission that occurs years into a program — hence the low-to-moderate confidence in (d) and the possibility of a June 13, 2033 admit-until date instead. On (e), the rule does not say what happens if CBP issues an F-2 I-94 later than the principal's date; 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)(E) is a substantive limit on the dependent's authorized stay but does not automatically amend the I-94, so a correction may be needed.
</submission>

PDF:               https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-03-27/pdf/2026-06017.pdf

Abstract:
The Department of Labor (DOL or the Department) is issuing this Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) to solicit comments and public input regarding its proposal to revise Employment and Training Administration (ETA) regulations governing the prevailing wages for employment opportunities that United States (U.S.) employers seek to fill with alien workers on a permanent or temporary basis through certain EB-2 and EB-3 employment-based immigrant visas via the Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) program or through H-1B, H-1B1, or E-3 nonimmigrant visas. Specifically, DOL is proposing to amend its regulations governing the PERM program and Labor Condition Applications (LCAs) to incorporate changes to the computation of wage levels under the Department's four-tiered prevailing wage structure based on the Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (OEWS) wage survey administered by the Department's Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). These proposed revisions aim to better align prevailing wage levels with the wages paid to U.S. workers who are similarly employed in the occupation and area of intended employment. The Department's proposed revisions also seek to strengthen program integrity by reducing the incentive for employers to use these programs to replace, rather than supplement, U.S. workers by employing lower-paid alien workers. In addition, the revision would enable the Department to more effectively ensure that the employment of immigrant and nonimmigrant workers admitted or otherwise provided one of the covered statuses does not adversely affect the wages and working conditions of U.S. workers.

tools.name: fr_search

query.description: Full-text search terms; "" for none. Supports quoted phrases, e.g. "\"extension of stay\" F-1".
query.title: Query

doc_type.description: Document types: RULE, PRORULE (proposed rule), NOTICE, PRESDOCU (presidential document). null for all.
doc_type.title: Doc Type

agency.description: Agency slugs, e.g. homeland-security-department, u-s-citizenship-and-immigration-services, u-s-immigration-and-customs-enforcement, state-department, labor-department, executive-office-of-the-president.
agency.title: Agency

pres_type.description: Presidential document subtypes (use with doc_type PRESDOCU).
pres_type.title: Pres Type

cfr.description: CFR title:part affected, e.g. 8:214. The part must be numeric; lettered parts are not supported by this filter.
cfr.title: Cfr

tools.description: Search U.S. Federal Register documents (rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents) by keywords and filters. Prints document numbers, titles, types, dates, citations, dockets, RINs and abstracts.

tools.name: fr_doc
tools.description: Metadata for one Federal Register document: title, type, action, citation, page range, publication/signing/effective dates, comment deadline, docket, RIN, CFR parts affected, corrections, abstract.

tools.name: fr_toc
tools.description: Outline of a document's full text: headings with line numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_grep

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.
pattern.title: Pattern

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).
context.title: Context

tools.description: Regex search inside one document's full text. Shows the lines of each match with line numbers, context lines and the FR page of each match. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_text
tools.description: Read a document's full text by line range, with line numbers. [[Page N]] markers give FR page numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

rationale.description: Brief evidence: what the submission says (quote or locate it) and any tool checks. Explain any 'unclear'.
